extracted.intended_audience: cognitive scientists, psychologists, and computational humor / AI researchers
extracted.subtask_description: A cognitive theory and computational proposal explaining humor comprehension as interactions between fast associative processes (System 1), slow deliberative processes (System 2), and emotional appraisals; includes criteria for joke design, individual and social moderators, and specifications for a domain-specific computational model (puns).

rubrics_metrics.name: Four-stage sequence of humor comprehension
rubrics_metrics.description: Mirth is created by a quick succession of four emotional and cognitive stages: surprise, reflection, dismissal, and compensation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The paper frames humor comprehension as resulting from complex interactions between multiple cognitive functions over a short period of time; converging evidence (brain imaging, facial studies, repetition effects, frustration smiles) supports the plausibility of this general pattern.

rubrics_metrics.name: Surprise stage (expectation violation)
rubrics_metrics.description: In the surprise stage, an expectation produced by the automatic System 1 is violated, leading to surprise and the engagement of the deliberate System 2.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Surprise is triggered when System 1 (associative and inflexible) fails to make sense of the input; this failure is the event that recruits the slower, more deliberate processing of System 2.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reflection stage (System 2 sense-making)
rubrics_metrics.description: In reflection, System 2 makes sense of the surprising stimulus through more elaborate, flexible, and time-consuming processing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reflection may involve heuristic searches, backtracking, removing and adding alternative interpretations, and relies on working memory capacity; longer reflection reduces processing fluency and can affect mirth.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dismissal stage (appraisal of irrelevance)
rubrics_metrics.description: In dismissal, the surprising stimulus is appraised as irrelevant and not worthy of further processing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The system inspects differences between the new and old solution and looks for reasons to dismiss the surprise (e.g., concluding a character was purposely misleading); dismissal reduces the negative valence of surprise and sets up compensation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Compensation stage (trampoline effect -> mirth)
rubrics_metrics.description: In compensation, as the mind adjusts from a slightly negative state to a positive state, a trampoline effect occurs producing an outburst of positive emotion (mirth).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compensation can be compounded by other factors such as superiority or the pleasure of epistemic discovery; the overall humor rating is influenced by factors from previous stages (e.g., time in reflection, strength of dismissal).

rubrics_metrics.name: Good joke crafting constraint (System1/System2 balance)
rubrics_metrics.description: A good joke must be difficult enough so System 1 does not understand it, and easy enough so System 2 does not take too much time to understand it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Joke-teller must 'walk a thin line'; using other appraisals, such as superiority, can increase funniness. This asymmetry explains why joke crafting is harder than understanding and why humor can signal intelligence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Processing fluency & repetition effects
rubrics_metrics.description: Repeated exposure can make a second encounter funnier due to processing fluency, but continued exposure will eventually train System 1 and the joke will be 'worn out'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The paper notes Topolinski (2014) and Belch & Belch (1984): initial repetition benefits (faster System 2 sense-making on second encounter) versus long-term decay as System 1 learns the joke.

rubrics_metrics.name: Social context modulates funniness
rubrics_metrics.description: Humor and laughter are significantly influenced by social setting (e.g., jokes are funnier when someone else is present; funniness increases with number of viewers).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Social functions include bonding among those who laugh together, alienation of the butt of the joke, and roles in mate selection; even imagined audiences can potentiate smiling.

rubrics_metrics.name: Individual differences in humor appreciation
rubrics_metrics.description: Individuals differ in preferred joke types and in humor comprehension; working memory capacity affects ability to appreciate complex jokes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The dual-process account explains high vs low comedy distinctions (high = thoughtful appreciation; low = spontaneous laughter). Lower working memory efficiency/capacity may make complex jokes less fluent and less funny for some people.

rubrics_metrics.name: Type-specific sources of surprise and solution methods
rubrics_metrics.description: Different joke types produce surprise via different mechanisms (e.g., puns: word-sense disambiguation; slapstick: sensory events like loud noises), and thus require different problem-solving techniques in reflection.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: puns require linguistic knowledge and word-sense disambiguation; farce/slapstick may rely on perceptual anomalies; computational modeling should account for these differences when targeting domains.

rubrics_metrics.name: Computational model success criterion (interpretation network completeness)
rubrics_metrics.description: Success is defined as completing an interpretation network where all story characters have intentions to support all actions they perform and each predicate node is related to at least one other predicate node.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The interpretation network is built from propositions/literals; success requires coherent intentional structure and connectivity among predicate nodes (example illustrated with 'I asked if I was a gifted child...').

rubrics_metrics.name: Architectural requirements for computational humor systems
rubrics_metrics.description: Implementing humor comprehension requires (1) acquiring required background knowledge and applying it at the right time, (2) implementing a system with multiple cognitive functions collaborating, and (3) modeling the correct temporal characteristics for interactions among functions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The paper emphasizes that these challenges make general-purpose humor understanding currently beyond AI capabilities; suggests domain-specific focus (e.g., puns) as tractable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Online vs offline processing behaviors in computational model
rubrics_metrics.description: Online mode (mimicking System 1) performs limited memory retrieval, selects only a few highest-activation elements, and disallows backtracking; offline mode (mimicking System 2) performs deliberate heuristic search, allows backtracking and alternative interpretations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Online failure (new predicate cannot connect) triggers surprise and transition to offline; offline can remove or add elements to the interpretation network to find a coherent solution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Humor strength metric (time vs dismissal weighting)
rubrics_metrics.description: Overall humor rating can be computed by weighing time spent in offline (reflective) mode against the strength of dismissal; more search time leads to less mirth, while a stronger reason for dismissal leads to stronger mirth.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This gives a quantitative intuition: extended reflection reduces processing fluency (reducing mirth), but strong dismissal (e.g., high absurdity) can amplify mirth in compensation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Falsifiable temporal-sequence predictions
rubrics_metrics.description: The theory predicts a temporal order: surprise happens earlier than System 2 engagement, which happens earlier than superiority; removing surprise should eliminate humor even if superiority is present.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These are experimentally testable (behavioral experiments, brain imaging, pupil-size measures); pupil dilation is suggested as indicator of System 2 activation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interpretation-network construction and retrieval dynamics
rubrics_metrics.description: As each proposition is read, a small semantic 'interpretation network' is constructed by retrieving nodes and edges from a larger background knowledge network; retrieved elements spread activation back into the background network and only a small number of highest-activation elements are retrieved.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Failure occurs when a new input predicate node cannot be connected to any other predicate nodes in the interpretation network (this operationalizes surprise); retrieval dynamics simulate associative, limited inference in System 1.
